'''Herchel Smith''' (May 6, 1925 – December 20, 2001<ref>{{Cite web |date=17 June 2002 |title=Reporter 19/6/02: Notice of a benefaction |url=https://www.admin.cam.ac.uk/reporter/2001-02/weekly/5889/4.html |access-date=18 March 2026 |website=[[University of Cambridge]]}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Herchel Smith gives Harvard $100 million |url=http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2002/04.25/08-smith.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041227104134/http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2002/04.25/08-smith.html |archive-date=27 December 2004 |website=[[Harvard Gazette]]}}</ref>) was an Anglo-American [[organic chemist]].  His discoveries include the key inventions underlying oral and injectable [[contraceptives]]. In later life, he was a major benefactor to university science. In England, the [[University of Cambridge]] and [[Queen Mary University of London]] have been the major beneficiaries; and in the US, [[Harvard University]], the [[University of Pennsylvania]], and [[Williams College]]. During his lifetime and after his death, Smith donated over US$200 million to Cambridge and US$100 million to Harvard, including endowments to expand student exchange between the two universities through [[Fellowship|fellowships]].

His early education in Plymouth<ref name=":0" /> and Exeter (in the South West of England) led him in 1942 to [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge]], where he studied the [[Natural Sciences Tripos]]. Smith had research interests in organic chemistry that were stimulated by Professor [[Lord Todd]].

His independent research started in [[Oxford University]] (1952–1956) but reached its full fruition whilst he was a lecturer in [[organic chemistry]] at the [[Victoria University of Manchester|University of Manchester]].

In 1961, a three-month visit to the research laboratories of [[Wyeth Pharmaceuticals]] in Pennsylvania, evolved into a permanent position where he continued to research steroid chemistry.

Herchel Smith's work on new methods for the total synthesis of [[steroids]] led to the development of commercially feasible methods for the industrial production of [[estrone]], [[equilin]] (an important constituent of treatments for [[menopause|post-menopausal syndrome]]), [[19-nortestosterone|19-nor-testosterone]], and [[Norgestrel]] (a novel [[progestogen]]). Norgestrel was found to be a potent contraceptive and formed the basis for a range of contraceptive drugs both oral and injectable.

He retired in 1973 and started a new career as a [[Philanthropy|philanthropist]] in which he returned to the academic community the major part of the substantial fortune that had accrued from his patent and licensing fees. One of his projects was funding Cambridge students to study postgraduate courses at Harvard, and Harvard students to study at Cambridge.<ref name=":0" />

== Personal life ==
Smith had a wife, Sheila, who pre-deceased him, and a son, Marcus.<ref name=":0" />
